RESPONSIVE BRIEF OF 
INDUSTRIAL CUSTOMER ORGANIZATIONS AND AMTRAK 
Pursuant to the Order on Show Cause Proceeding, Directing Compliance Filings, 
Establishing Paper Hearing, and Granting In Part and Denying In Part Complaint (“Order”) in the 
above-captioned dockets,1 and the January 23, 2026, Notice of Extension of Time,2 the PJM 
Industrial Customer Coalition (“PJMICC”), the Industrial Energy Consumers of America 
(“IECA”), the American Forest and Paper Association (“AF&PA”) (collectively, “Industrials”), 
and the National Railroad Passenger Corporation (“Amtrak”) hereby file this Responsive Brief in 
response to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) and the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners’ 
(“PJM Transmission Owners”) Initial Briefs in Docket No. EL25-49, et al. (“Initial Briefs”)3, 
which were filed at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”) on 
February 23, 2026, in the above-captioned dockets.

2 Notice of Extension of Time, Docket Nos. EL25-49-000, EL25-49-001, AD24-11-000, EL25-20-000 (Jan. 23, 2026).

I.
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 
As retail customers with high energy consumption needs, the Industrials/Amtrak have long 
endorsed customer choice as a foundational principle for electric service. As such, the 
Industrials/Amtrak appreciate the promise of new transmission services designed to support the 
type and amount of service required by customers. Lessons can be learned from the optionality in 
the natural gas industry, while also recognizing the utility’s obligation to serve and the right of 
industrial, institutional, and transportation customers to receive reliable electric service under 
various federal and state laws. The proposed implementation of PJM’s three new transmission 
services (“New Services”) may yield benefits and optionality, but the New Services must be just, 
reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory or preferential under Section 206 of the Federal Power 
Act.4 Consequently, implementation of the New Services requires careful consideration of 
regulatory and jurisdictional issues and adherence to cost-causation principles. As the Commission 
develops the details for the New Services, the Industrials/Amtrak emphasize the following:  
1) A just and reasonable back-up service is missing from the new transmission services 
structure. Back-up service provided without a default assumption that it will be used during 
system peaks is guaranteed to Qualifying Facilities (“QF”) under the Public Utility 
Regulatory Policies Act of 1978 (“PURPA”) and should be extended to other retail 
customers with on-site generation on a cost-causation basis, either through retail netting or 
through a firm, back-up service charged on a cost-causation basis (“cost-based”).  
2) The outcome of PJM’s pending compliance proposal in FERC Docket No. ER26-1479 
(“BTMG Compliance Docket”) regarding PJM’s retail Behind-the-Meter Generation 
(“BTMG”) applicability rules, including a yet-to-be-determined materiality threshold 
(“Retail Threshold”), directly impacts and relates to the New Services and whether the 
terms and conditions of the New Services are just and reasonable. While specific eligibility 
for retail netting is under consideration in the BTMG Compliance Docket, no firm cost-
based back-up service has been proposed in the instant proceeding. 
3) The Commission should incorporate incentives for Co-Located Load to bring new 
generation, with appropriate inducements for such generation’s reliable operation. 
4 16 U.S.C. § 824e(a).

3
4) The terms for New Services must respect state/federal jurisdictional boundaries and 
clearly translate into transparent retail rates. 
Industrial retail configurations are varied, complex, and unique. Generally, in contrast to 
typical computational loads, industrial customers produce a physical product on-site; cannot shift 
load to other facilities; often must continue to operate for safety and environmental compliance 
reasons; and frequently have generation and load deeply integrated via cogeneration, a process that 
generates both electric power and useful thermal energy.5 Traditional industrial load 
configurations with BTMG also provide substantial benefits to the grid—this traditional, existing 
customer load did not trigger the current resource adequacy challenges on the grid, nor does it 
present the reliability risks posed by super-sized loads rapidly seeking to come online today. In the 
BTMG Compliance Docket, the Industrials/Amtrak submitted the Affidavit of James R. 
Dauphinais (“Dauphinais Affidavit”), in which Mr. Dauphinais provided testimony concerning the 
configurations of industrial, institutional, and transportation retail customers, particularly QFs, and 
the technical and regulatory basis for ensuring such customers have access to back-up power at 
just and reasonable rates.6
In contrast to the “traditional” load described above, computational loads (including data 
centers) do not generally have substantial cogeneration, typically do not operate large motors 
(which can help with grid stability), can turn on and off nearly instantaneously, and can reach 
extremely large sizes, well beyond most traditional industrial and institutional retail customers. 
The size and scale of the computational load currently in the planning process across PJM is

energy and forms of useful thermal energy (such as heat or steam), used for industrial, commercial, heating, or cooling 
purposes, through the sequential use of energy.” 18 C.F.R. § 292.202(c). 
6 See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Joint Protest and Comments of Industrial Customer Organizations and Amtrak, 
Docket No. ER26-1479-000 (Mar. 16, 2026) (“Industrials/Amtrak Protest”), Exhibit No. IA-1. The Dauphinais 
Affidavit is attached to this filing as Attachment 1 and provides support for the arguments herein.

4
massive, both in the size of individual facilities and in the scale of the projects coming online 
across the PJM footprint.  
As most planned load growth is driven by load additions greater than 300 MW, the 
Industrials/Amtrak proposed in the BTMG Compliance Docket a Retail Threshold of at least 200 
MW, under which BTMG netting should continue.7 The Industrials/Amtrak also proposed that 
QFs maintain their continued eligibility for BTMG netting, in accordance with PURPA 
requirements.8 If the FERC accepts these proposals, it will go a long way toward resolving the 
concerns about back-up power in the design of the New Services. However, if the FERC denies 
the Industrials/Amtrak’s proposals in the BTMG Compliance Docket, the lack of back-up service 
in the design of the New Services becomes a heightened concern.  
Retail customers represented by the Industrials/Amtrak in this docket seldom grab 
headlines and are often not at the center of large-load and transmission planning discussions 
today—yet they have operated such systems reliably for decades. The transmission system has 
grown up around such traditional loads, worked in concert with them, and benefited from their 
presence, operations, and long-term planning. As explained further in Section III, infra, these retail 
BTMG configurations are varied and diverse. The facts of on-site generation configurations matter 
and must be understood to ensure just and reasonable determinations in this proceeding.  
Examples are plentiful. For some retail customers, industrial processes with cogeneration 
and combined heat and power (“CHP”) assets may require steam heat produced from the 
generation, meaning if the generation goes down, the load follows. In that case, it would defy cost-
causation principles to require such a facility to pay for transmission services it cannot physically

8 Id. at 17-23.

5
use (such as via a Grid Reliance Charge as proposed in the PJM Transmission Owners’ Initial 
Brief).9
Other industrial customers currently qualify, or could qualify, as QFs under PURPA, 
granting them the right to back-up and maintenance power at rates/terms that do not assume that 
units will be down during system peaks and do not assume that units will be down at the same time 
as the other QFs (unless there is data backing that assumption). Yet, as will be explained further 
herein, the current proposed design of the New Services in the Initial Briefs makes no allowance 
for back-up power at cost-based rates. 
A third example is that, as a legacy of the buildout of the Northeast Corridor (NEC), 
Amtrak requires service at 25 Hz, which it receives, at least for some of its requirements, through 
a contractual arrangement with a third-party generator that is neither a small power production QF 
nor a cogeneration QF. This arrangement provides the only black-start capability for Amtrak’s 
south end of its Northeast Corridor traction power system if the 60 Hz power grid goes out of 
service. 
Each of these configurations, plus others, is described in greater detail in Section III, infra. 
These configurations underscore the critical need for the FERC to consider the impact on 
traditional large-load configurations to ensure a just and reasonable replacement rate when 
authorizing a final design for the New Services. Absent a just and reasonable method of obtaining 
back-up power, many retail customers will face devastating economic consequences. For some, as 
further explained below and in the Dauphinais Affidavit, it will mean closure of generating units, 
exacerbating the current resource adequacy concerns in the region. 
9 PJM Transmission Owners Initial Brief at 5, 11.

6
With careful attention to the reasons, needs, and cost-causation basis for back-up service, 
this result is avoidable. The Commission can authorize the New Services while also ensuring a 
just and reasonable back-up service is in place for QFs and other similarly situated retail customers. 
Accordingly, the Industrials/Amtrak respectfully request that the Commission develop the New 
Services, consistent with the comments and changes recommended herein, to ensure the avoidance 
of unintended and irreparable damage to America’s essential manufacturing sector and 
institutional and transportation service providers.
II.
BACKGROUND 
On December 18, 2025, the Commission issued the Order, finding that the PJM Tariff is 
unjust and unreasonable due to the lack of specificity for the rates, terms, and conditions that apply 
to Co-Located Load and directing PJM to make several compliance and informational filings. The 
Order directed PJM to create three New Services, including an interim, non-firm Network 
Integration Transmission Service (“Interim NITS”), a Firm Contract Demand Service (“Firm 
CDS”), and a Non-Firm Contract Demand Service (“Non-Firm CDS”).10 Paper hearing procedures 
were established to evaluate the rates, terms, and conditions of the New Services.  
The Order also addressed PJM’s retail BTMG rules, which have long allowed for 
measurement of a retail customer’s transmission (as well as capacity, energy and ancillary 
services) cost responsibility by actual use of the system as measured at the meter. In light of its 
finding that “circumstances have changed since the Commission approved PJM’s retail BTMG 
rules,” the Commission directed PJM to implement changes to BTMG rules above a yet-to-be-
determined materiality threshold (“Retail Threshold”).11 PJM, the Industrials/Amtrak, and others 
10 Order at P 2. 
11 Order at P 186.

7
have subsequently made various proposals for the Retail Threshold and other proposed terms for 
retail BTMG rules in the BTMG Compliance Docket. 
On February 23, 2026, PJM and the PJM Transmission Owners filed Initial Briefs in the 
above-captioned dockets, kicking off the briefing stage of the Paper Hearing.12 PJM also convened 
several stakeholder workshops to solicit input on the design and pricing of the New Services.13
To provide additional perspective on issues set for the Paper Hearing, and to respond to 
proposals made in the Initial Briefs, the Industrials/Amtrak respectfully offer the following 
response for the Commission’s consideration.  
III.
THE INDUSTRIALS/AMTRAK 
This Responsive Brief is being filed on behalf of many of the major American energy 
consumers in the PJM region: industrial customers that manufacture products used in everyday 
life and commerce; a provider of core transportation services across the nation; and institutions 
that offer essential medical and educational services. In many cases, these traditional institutional, 
industrial, and transportation customers own or operate their own generation—not because energy 
is their primary industry, but because their core work is energy-intensive. These customers have 
elected to construct or contract for retail BTMG in order to control their own energy costs, create 
efficiencies, and/or address reliability needs. Even though the Order was issued largely in response 
to the impacts of “super-sized” loads such as data centers on the grid, the resulting changes (as 
currently proposed in the Initial Briefs) will directly and deeply impact these traditional retail

customers. Like all other retail customers, manufacturers, hospitals, universities, and 
transportation providers have the same right to just and reasonable rates that are grounded in cost-
causation principles. 
The Industrials, which include several associations of leading American manufacturing 
companies and other energy-intensive customers, represent well over $1 trillion in sales, including 
thousands of manufacturing facilities and millions of family-sustaining jobs in the United States. 
As an industry, manufacturing is unique compared to all other sectors, employing over 15 million 
people in the United States14 and contributing $2.3 trillion to U.S. Gross Domestic Product 
(“GDP”) in 2023 (amounting to 10.2% of total U.S. GDP, measured in chained 2017 dollars).15
Manufacturers produce the raw materials and inputs necessary for sustaining commerce and our 
overall standard of living. Manufacturers are energy-intensive, frequently operate 24/7, are price-
sensitive, and compete globally. Unlike the surge in large-load demands from data centers and 
computational workloads, most manufacturers are simply trying to remain competitive and keep 
their facilities operational and financially healthy amid ever-rising operational costs. Expansions 
of existing facilities are carried out over years of deliberate planning. Small changes in electricity 
prices can have significant impacts on the competitiveness of existing facilities and serious 
implications for reshoring and expanding facilities and production capabilities in the United States.  
Amtrak is a corporation authorized by the Rail Passenger Service Act of 1970, codified at 
49 U.S.C. §§ 24101, et seq. Amtrak provides passenger rail service across the continental United 
States, including within the PJM footprint. Amtrak consumes substantial amounts of electricity in

operations. While Amtrak is not a manufacturer, it is an industrial customer of utility services. For 
many years, Amtrak has harnessed retail BTMG within PJM to support its business operations and 
reliability imperatives. Amtrak’s interests align with the Industrials and reflect the wide-ranging 
types of bespoke retail BTMG arrangements that support the region’s and the nation’s economy.  
The issues set for Paper Hearing carry great weight for retail customers like Amtrak and 
members of the Industrials. If the FERC determines in the BTMG Compliance Docket that existing 
industrial, institutional, and transportation applications no longer qualify as BTMG and, as such, 
customers no longer have their cost responsibility for transmission (and possibly capacity) 
measured at the meter, these customers will be reliant on the FERC to ensure there are adequate 
transmission services, grounded in cost-causation principles, to enable these customers to remain 
economic. If the requirements and standards for the New Services are inadequately designed, 
existing concerns about resource adequacy and cost causation will deepen. Such a result would 
risk rendering uneconomic a vast array of existing on-site generation arrangements. This may have 
devastating economic impacts on industrial customers, who, as noted by PJM in the BTMG 
Compliance Docket, may decide to shutter their on-site generating units, exacerbating the resource 
adequacy challenges.16
Further impacting the cost and regulatory analysis, it is important to recognize that 
industrial retail configurations are varied, complex, and unique. In contrast to typical 
computational and data center load, industrial customers: (a) produce a physical product on-site; 
(b) typically cannot shift load to other facilities; (c) often must continue to operate for safety and 
environmental compliance reasons; (d) frequently have generation and load deeply integrated via

cogeneration; and (e) often provide valuable resource adequacy and reliability benefits to the 
broader grid. These traditional load configurations are neither the essential cause of the current 
resource adequacy challenges on the grid, nor do they present the reliability risks posed by super-
sized, inverter-based loads rapidly seeking to come online today. In fact, they provide substantial 
reliability and resource adequacy benefits to the grid.17 In contrast, the new computational loads 
entering the grid today do not have substantial cogeneration,18 do not typically operate large motors 
(which, in some cases, help with stability on the grid),19 can turn off and on nearly instantaneously, 
and can reach extremely large sizes (“super-sized”), well beyond most traditional industrial and 
institutional retail customers. As most planned load growth is driven by load greater than 300 MW, 
the Industrials/Amtrak proposed a Retail Threshold in the BTMG Compliance Docket of at least 
200 MW, under which BTMG netting should continue.20
The above-listed characteristics of “traditional” large loads have direct implications for 
how cost causation, grid risks, and other considerations should be evaluated. The Commission’s

allocation transparency; and (d) whether retail customers can access cost-based (and in many 
cases, legally-required) back-up service.  
Industrial, institutional, and transportation customers with on-site generation are rarely in 
the news and are often not at the center of large load and transmission planning discussions; the 
reason for this is that they have operated such on-site generation systems reliably for decades. The 
transmission system has grown up around such traditional loads, works in concert with them, and 
benefits from their presence and operation. The facts of on-site generation configurations matter 
and must be understood to make just and reasonable determinations in this docket. The following 
are several examples of configurations that raise specific applicability and interpretation questions: 

If a cogeneration facility and its associated manufacturing load is required to operate 
as a Co-Location Arrangement, the manufacturing load’s actual use of the transmission 
system may not equate to the actual maximum amount of load on-site, as the industrial 
process may require steam heat produced from the generation, meaning if the 
generation goes down, the load follows—in that case, it would defy cost causation 
principles to require such a facility to pay for transmission services it cannot physically 
use (such as via a Grid Reliance Charge as proposed in the PJM Transmission Owners’ 
Initial Brief).21

Amtrak, a retail customer, has a contractual arrangement for retail BTMG to support 
its Northeast Corridor operations. As a legacy of the buildout of the Northeast Corridor, 
Amtrak requires service at 25 Hz, which it receives, at least for some of its 
requirements, through a contractual arrangement with a third-party generator that is 
neither a small power production QF nor a cogeneration QF. This arrangement provides 
the only black-start capability for Amtrak’s south end of its Northeast Corridor traction 
power system if the 60 Hz power grid goes out of service. 

Many industrials currently qualify, or could qualify, as QFs under PURPA, granting 
them the right to back-up and maintenance power at rates/terms that do not assume that

units will be down during system peaks and do not assume that units will be down at 
the same time as the other QFs (unless there is data backing that assumption). Yet, as 
explained further herein, the current proposed design of the Contract Demand Services 
(“CDS”) in the Initial Briefs makes no allowance for back-up power at cost-based rates. 

An industrial customer represented by the Industrials has several dozen combined heat 
and power (“CHP”) assets, totaling between 80 MW and 200 MW in production 
capacity, fueled by a mixture of coal and natural gas; the CHP assets are primarily 
designed to meet the thermal load; thermal energy is required for industrial processes; 
when a significant decrease in electricity generation occurs, thermal generation also 
declines, resulting in a simultaneous load shedding event decreasing the need for any 
external electricity purchases; there are physical limitations on amounts of power that 
can be drawn from the grid; a standby service contract is in force, with decades of 
demand history informing the contract; a purchased power contract has been in effect 
for decades, as well, and is renewed on a year-to-year basis.22

Many other examples exist of bespoke arrangements for industrial and institutional 
customers that may require firm back-up needs. As explained in the Dauphinais 
Affidavit, some of these units, particularly cogeneration units, are highly efficient and 
highly reliable units, requiring limited downtime.23
Each of these configurations underscores the critical need for the FERC to consider the 
impact on traditional large load customers when authorizing a final design for the New Services. 
Due to the above examples and others, there are sound legal, regulatory, and cost-based reasons 
that industrial and institutional applications should qualify for cost-based back-up power options, 
whether through retail BTMG netting eligibility, or, alternatively, through a firm, cost-based back-
up and maintenance service. Further, the New Services should be structured to support Bring Your 
Own New Generation initiatives and to create efficient investment signals, as the industry faces a 
crisis of resource adequacy. Finally, any New Services design finalized by the FERC should ensure 
sufficient clarity as to how cost responsibility will be assigned to retail customers, while respecting 
state jurisdiction over retail rates.

To that end, the Industrials/Amtrak respectfully request that the Commission consider the 
following arguments in determining rates, terms, and conditions of the New Services. With the 
changes recommended herein, the Commission can approve rules that effectuate the goals of the 
Order while avoiding unintended damage to America’s essential manufacturing sector and 
institutional and transportation service providers. 
IV.
ARGUMENTS 
A.
A just and reasonable back-up service is missing from the new transmission 
services structure. A cost-based back-up service is guaranteed to Qualifying 
Facilities under PURPA and should be extended to other retail customers with 
on-site generation on a cost-causation basis.  
The New Services represent a significant change to how transmission services are 
designed, bundled, and paid in the PJM region. However, as currently proposed, the New Services 
are missing a critical component. The current design lacks a back-up service that is based on cost-
causation and that meets the legal requirements of PURPA. Back-up service is an essential 
component of energy management for many industrials and other retail customers with on-site 
generation, including QFs, which are guaranteed access to back-up service with specific cost-based 
assumptions.24
Because neither the New Services nor NITS calculated on a gross basis meet these 
requirements, as explained below, at a bare minimum, QFs should retain access to longstanding 
retail BTMG netting rules. If the FERC determines otherwise, however, the FERC should ensure 
QFs have access to a cost-based back-up service. Retail customers with BTMG that is not a QF 
should also, based on principles of cost causation, be provided with access to cost-based back-up 
services, either through NITS with netting or through a cost-based back-up service. Access to 
24 18 C.F.R. § 292.305.

14
back-up services is a critical component to allowing industrial, institutional, and transportation 
retail customers to continue to operate without significant economic damage, including likely 
closures of some BTMG generating units.   
1.
PURPA ensures that QFs have access to back-up and maintenance 
service that meets assumptions about generator uptime, and the NITS 
netting construct meets this requirement. 
Congress passed PURPA in 1978 to encourage cogeneration, small power production, and 
geothermal energy production.25 PURPA has played an important role for manufacturers and the 
electric grid for nearly five decades, providing market access where none previously existed, 
taking strain off the grid, and supporting American industry by enabling economic means to reduce 
energy costs. Under PURPA, QFs fall into two broad categories: “qualifying small power 
production facilities,” which can be sized up to 80 MW, and “qualifying cogeneration facilities,” 
which have no size limit.26 Cogeneration QFs must achieve certain efficiency standards and are 
highly efficient in their use of input fuels. Cogeneration QFs, which produce both electricity and 
heat from the same fuel source, make use of the “waste heat” in their manufacturing, heating, or 
cooling process. As explained by Mr. Dauphinais in the attached Affidavit (which was filed in the 
BTMG Compliance Docket), “Cogeneration Facilities can achieve efficiencies in excess of 80%, 
by using waste heat and avoiding electrical losses, compared to the efficiency of approximately 
50% for conventional electricity generation with a steam boiler.”27
Under FERC regulations (enacted at Congress’ direction), QFs are entitled to access to 
supplementary power, back-up power, maintenance power, and interruptible power, pursuant to 
25 16 U.S. Code § 824a-3(a). 
26 16 U.S. Code § 824a-3. “Qualifying small power production facilities” are also referred to as “small power 
production QFs,” and “qualifying cogeneration facilities” are also referred to as “cogeneration QFs.” 
27 Dauphinais Affidavit at P 11.

long-established enacting regulations.28 “Back-up power” is defined in the regulations as “electric 
energy or capacity supplied by an electric utility to replace energy ordinarily generated by a 
facility’s own generation equipment during an unscheduled outage of the facility.”29
Critically, rates for back-up or maintenance power “[s]hall not be based upon an 
assumption (unless supported by factual data) that forced outages or other reductions in electric 
output by all qualifying facilities on an electric utility’s system will occur simultaneously, or 
during the system peak, or both.”30 As explained by Mr. Dauphinais, the current BTMG netting 
construct for NITS permits QFs to receive the back-up power they are guaranteed—back-up power 
that is charged without a default assumption that the back-up power will be needed during peak 
times.31 If back-up services are needed during peak times, the current NITS design ensures 
customers pay for them by appropriately measuring peak usage.32 As explained by Mr. Dauphinais, 
“With respect to the transmission component of back-up and maintenance power, Section 34.2 of 
the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff (“PJM Tariff”) currently excludes the load served by 
the operating behind the meter generation of a retail customer from that retail customer’s daily 
load for [NITS].”33 He further states:  
Whether a retail customer has behind the meter generation or not, its NITS 
charges are based on the demand the retail customer has historically put on the 
transmission system at the time of the annual peak of the transmission pricing

1. Hourly, actual use calculation – no standby fee. As an as-available service, Non-
Firm CDS should not be charged a standby fee. Regardless of the merits of a standby 
fee in context of a firm service offering, a standby fee does not make sense when it 
charges for “access” with no guarantee that such access will actually be available. 
Rather, an actual use calculation on an hourly basis would be an appropriate way to 
charge for Non-Firm CDS. Such an approach guarantees that retail customers pay for 
what they use; such revenues collected by transmission owners would go toward the 
revenue requirement for that transmission owner, ultimately lowering rates for Firm 
CDS and NITS customers. 
2. No transmission planning based on Non-Firm CDS. As a non-firm, as-available 
service, Non-Firm CDS should not be considered as a factor in transmission planning. 
If transmission owners planned for additional transmission capacity for Non-Firm 
CDS, the costs of that transmission capacity would have to be recovered through rates. 
This cost recovery would have the effect of raising rates for other transmission 
customers, because Non-Firm CDS, by design, should be less expensive than its Firm 
CDS and NITS cousins. 
3. Fuel contracts. Co-Located Load subscribing to Non-Firm CDS should have firm 
natural gas capacity or other adequate alternatives to be able to utilize Non-Firm CDS. 
The Commission should include such reasonable requirements to avoid misuse of the 
Non-Firm CDS service by generators who have the ability to operate but may want to 
rely on the grid when it appears to be more economical for that generator. From a 
resource adequacy perspective, policies surrounding Non-Firm CDS should encourage 
Bring Your Own New Generation, which promotes building and operating on-site 
generation. 
4. Anti-manipulation. Non-Firm CDS should have clearly defined allowable 
circumstances or standards for load to reserve non-firm transmission service. To 
preserve and support resource adequacy on the broader grid during times of system 
stress, switching from use of on-site generation to grid-supplied resources via Non-
Firm CDS should not be for short-term economic reasons (such as when pricing for a 
grid resource is lower than the on-site generation resource). Acknowledging efficiency 
gains from letting markets operate on economic signals, Non-Firm CDS should 
generally be available only if generation is unavailable for physical reasons—planned 
maintenance, fuel outages, etc.—especially during times of system stress.

C.
A durable solution must provide clear direction on cost allocation while 
respecting federal-state jurisdictional distinctions. 
With the sweeping, transformative changes initiated by the Order, it is critical to ensure 
retail customers have clear, accountable, and understandable rates and terms for these services. 
This is particularly a concern considering interstate transmission services (the subject of this 
docket) are a federal-jurisdictional service, yet the service must be translated to retail rates and 
billed by Load-Serving Entities (“LSE”) or local distribution utilities.  
Many distribution utilities across PJM’s footprint publish methodologies of how customer 
cost responsibility is calculated in the Attachment M-2s filed with the PJM Tariff at FERC. It is 
not immediately clear from the Order how the retail cost allocation will be determined. Along 
those lines, the FERC must ensure that transmission owners’ calculation of individual customer 
and zonal transmission cost allocation is transparent, whether through an Attachment M-2 filing 
or another publicly transparent and accountable method. Clear direction on how charges for New 
Services will be established is necessary for a durable final order in this proceeding. A simple 
example of a lack of clarity would be a transmission owner that does not post its allocation 
methodology in a publicly-available way.

What are Cogeneration Facilities? 
 
5. 
FERC defines a Cogeneration Facility to be “equipment used to produce electric 
energy and forms of useful thermal energy (such as heat or steam), used for industrial, 
commercial, heating, or cooling purposes, through the sequential use of energy”.3  Given that on 
a combined basis these facilities provide both thermal and electric energy, cogeneration facilities 
are also commonly referred to as Combined Heat and Power (“CHP”) facilities. 
6. 
There are two types of Cogeneration Facilities – Topping-Cycle Cogeneration 
Facilities and Bottoming-Cycle Cogeneration Facilities. 
7. 
FERC defines a Topping-Cycle Cogeneration Facility as “a cogeneration facility 
in which the energy input to the facility is first used to produce useful power output, and at least 
some of the reject heat from the power production process is then used to provide useful thermal 
energy”.4  A common example of a Topping-Cycle Cogeneration Facility would be a facility 
with combustion turbine generation fired by natural gas, combustible waste gases, or some 
combination of the two, that produces electricity and provides steam for heating, cooling, and/or 
industrial processes via heat recovery steam generators that collect waste heat from the 
combustion turbine generator.  Another example would be a facility with boilers fired by fossil

Cogeneration Efficiency 
10. 
As I have noted, FERC’s definition of Cogeneration Facility requires the 
“sequential use of energy”.8  Specifically, for a Topping-Cycle Cogeneration Facility, FERC 
requires “the use of reject heat from a power production process in sufficient amounts in a 
thermal application or process to conform to the requirements of the operating standard”,9 where 
the “operating standard” is “the useful thermal energy output of the facility must be no less than 
5 percent of the total energy output during the 12-month period beginning with the date the 
facility first produces electric energy, and any calendar year subsequent to the year in which the 
facility first produces electric energy.”10  For a Bottoming-Cycle Cogeneration Facility, FERC 
requires “the use of reject heat from a thermal application or process, at least some of which is 
then used for power production”. 
11. 
Cogeneration Facilities, which, as I have noted, are also commonly referred to as 
CHP systems, are typically highly efficient because they capture heat that would otherwise be 
wasted and avoid electrical losses by generating electricity at the location where it will largely, if 
not entirely, be consumed.  Specifically, Cogeneration Facilities can achieve efficiencies in 
excess of 80%, by using waste heat and avoiding electrical losses, compared to the efficiency of 
approximately 50% for conventional electricity generation with a steam boiler.11

power well below the level that the retail customer needs for its electrical load.  This requires 
that the retail customer be able to purchase supplementary (or supplemental) electric power to 
cover the deficit from either a utility under a regulated retail electric service rate or from the 
wholesale power market through a retail supplier at just and reasonable rates where retail 
customer choice is available.

III. 
COMMERCIAL, INDUSTRIAL AND INSTITUTIONAL CUSTOMERS USING 
COGENERATION ARE NOT THE SAME AS VERY LARGE 
COMPUTATIONAL LOADS CO-LOCATED BEHIND THE METER OF 
GENERATION FACILITIES 
   
22. 
Very large computational loads co-located behind the meter of generation 
facilities are not similarly situated to traditional large commercial, industrial and institutional 
loads using Cogeneration Facilities located behind their meter. 
23. 
In particular, very large computational loads by their very nature generally do not 
have a high thermal energy need relative to the magnitude of their total electric load and do not 
produce large amounts of waste heat relative to the magnitude of their total electrical load.  As 
such, they are not candidates for Cogeneration Facilities beyond potentially addressing their 
cooling and heating needs. 
24. 
Thus, very large computational load processes are generally not highly thermally 
integrated, if integrated at all, with the co-located generation facilities whose meter they may be 
located behind.  This is because those generation facilities will either not be Cogeneration 
Facilities or be Cogeneration Facilities of greatly limited electrical capability relative to the total 
magnitude of the electrical load of their host retail customer. 
25. 
Without such integration, the co-located generation facilities will not provide the 
efficiency benefits that are provided by Cogeneration Facilities in serving commercial, industrial, 
and institutional customers.  In addition, depending on the specific nature of the co-located 
generation facilities, the generation may be operated only intermittently rather than at the high 
capacity factor typically required of Cogeneration Facilities to ensure their host retail customer 
thermal process needs are being reliably fully met.

Schedule 8 of the PJM Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load Serving Entities in the

customer’s capacity requirement is based the retail customer’s demand placed on the PJM 
market at the time of the summer coincident peak, just like it is for retail customers who do not 
have behind the meter generation.  Hence, whether a retail customer has behind the meter 
generation or not, its PJM capacity requirement is based on the demand the retail customer has

70.

 Very large computational loads co-located behind the meter of generation 
facilities are not similarly situated to traditional large commercial, 
industrial, and institutional loads using Cogeneration Facilities located 
behind their meter, as very large computational loads generally are not 
highly thermally integrated with any co-located generation facilities. 
 
 For traditional large loads served by Cogeneration Facilities, PJM’s

charges and capacity requirements are consistent with cost causation

when outages will occur and whether they will occur simultaneously.

Demand Transmission Service are not capable – either alone or in tandem

retail customers that utilize Qualifying Cogeneration Facilities at rates 
consistent with cost causation principles and FERC’s rules for providing 
backup and maintenance service to Qualifying Facilities.
